review:
Modbox, developed and published by Alientrap, occupies an interesting space between game and creative toolkit, offering players a flexible sandbox where the primary objective is not to complete predefined goals but to invent their own experiences. It is less concerned with delivering a curated adventure and more focused on giving players the means to experiment, build, and interact within a physics-driven environment. From the outset, it becomes clear that this is not a traditional game in the usual sense, but rather a platform that depends heavily on player imagination to reach its full potential.

At its core, the experience revolves around creation. Players are placed into an open 3D environment and given a broad set of tools that allow them to manipulate objects, construct scenarios, and design interactive systems. One of the most notable aspects of the game is its visual scripting feature, which enables users to define behaviors and logic without requiring formal coding knowledge. This system opens the door to a surprising level of complexity, allowing for the creation of mini-games, puzzles, or experimental mechanics. While this flexibility is one of the game’s greatest strengths, it also places a certain expectation on the player to actively engage with its systems rather than passively consume content.

The physics engine plays a central role in shaping the experience, providing a consistent and often playful foundation for experimentation. Objects react naturally to forces and interactions, encouraging players to test ideas, build contraptions, and explore cause-and-effect relationships. This sense of physicality becomes particularly compelling in virtual reality, where direct interaction with the environment enhances immersion and makes even simple actions feel tactile and engaging. The VR implementation is one of the game’s defining features, turning the sandbox into something that feels closer to a hands-on creative space than a conventional digital environment.

Multiplayer functionality adds another dimension, allowing players to share their creations and collaborate in real time. This transforms the sandbox from a solitary workshop into a social playground, where ideas can be developed collectively or experienced together. Whether constructing elaborate setups or participating in user-created activities, the presence of other players can significantly enhance the overall experience. Integration with community sharing systems further expands the available content, offering access to a range of creations that help mitigate the absence of structured, built-in gameplay.

Despite its strengths, Modbox is not without its challenges. The reliance on player-driven content means that the experience can feel sparse for those who are not inclined toward creation. Without a strong set of predefined activities or guided objectives, new players may struggle to find direction, especially in the early stages. Additionally, while the tools are powerful, they are not always immediately intuitive, and mastering them can require a degree of patience and experimentation. This learning curve can be a barrier, particularly for players expecting a more accessible or immediately rewarding experience.

Another factor that shapes the overall impression of the game is its development state. Having spent a long period in Early Access with relatively limited ongoing updates, it can feel somewhat static compared to other sandbox platforms that have continued to evolve over time. The foundation is solid, but there is a lingering sense that the game could have grown into something more expansive with additional support and refinement. This does not diminish what is already present, but it does highlight a gap between potential and realization.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and functional style that prioritizes usability over artistic ambition. The environments and assets are designed to support creativity rather than stand out on their own, resulting in a presentation that is clear but somewhat plain. In VR, this simplicity works to the game’s advantage, making interaction straightforward and reducing visual clutter. On desktop, however, the lack of visual flair can make the experience feel more like a toolset than a fully immersive game world.

In the end, Modbox is best understood as a creative platform that offers a wide range of possibilities without dictating how they should be used. It provides the tools for players to build and explore, but it leaves the responsibility of finding meaning and enjoyment largely in their hands. For those who enjoy experimentation and user-generated content, it can be a deeply engaging and rewarding space. For others seeking structured gameplay or a more guided experience, it may feel incomplete or difficult to fully connect with.

This is pretty crazy; I feel like I'm playing a mash-up of Dreams, Garry's Mod, Game Builder Garage and Minetest. In short, it's a creative person's dream mod simulator, but it feels almost like a complete game engine with prebuilt objects and visual scripting. 

I'm sure I've only scraped the surface in my adventures, so this review will absolutely be updated in the future, but my lengthy 7+ hour first impression has been nothing but "Wow, that's surprisingly deep". There's a lot of interesting potential in the realms of 3D modelling, voxel sculpting, scripting, modding and borderline prototypal game development all right inside of a neat little 'mod' box.

Also, I was surprised that it runs on all of my (admittedly lo-spec) systems without any issues; even my best setup falls way under the recommended system requirements and I can build anything I want without losing frames or having anything go south. This thing is extremely optimized, and you don't see that everyday.

This game is honestly one of the best games I've played in a while. It's left an impact on my life as well as my friend's. It may seem like it's lame due to the graphics in some places, but put on some intense music and hop into Gravity Gun Deathmatch with some friends, you'll see what i mean.
The building mechanics for Gravity Gun Deathmatch are so fun to use, especially paired with the concrete building sound effect that's in the game. If you really want to crank up the fun, add an Expanded Environments Pack and then try out Hellscape or Acid Rain as your Environment while you play, firing explosive barrels at eachother. I also really love the explosion effect that was given to the barrels on this one, it gives it a very nice feel.
Another Favorite of mine is the Bar Fight(found in the community tab). It's so much fun to just chaotically get 3 friends or so in the game and go absolutley crazy with it. The sound effects again, for this one are very fitting, with chaotic sounds of metal clanking and people hitting eachother. It's great to go crazy in.
About the actual game itself, it's made very well. You can see that effort was put in, even though it's still in Early Access. The Building Mechanics are almost uncomparable to gmod. The UI is actually really great. Simple, minimalistic style, easy to look at and understand. I can really build anything I'd like in modbox, which I know is not a new thing, as it's existed in popular titles such as Gmod, but this is a very well made and more up to date game.
As it says on the store, this game is also made for VR. It's made very well for vr, and it's great and unique that this is a game for both PC and VR. It is made very well on pc, as well as it's made for virtual reality. It really pushes the possibilities and shows what can be done. 
If you want to know more about what you can actually create in ModBox, you can see many examples in their trailers of how the game works, especially their recent 2.0 trailer. You can build anything using the built-in assets provided, and it feels pretty much limitless. There's of course also programming and settings elements, as i've played with putting sound effects in the game, changing environments, making chracters do specific things, invisible walls, giant scoreboards, the list can go on, this game is practically endless. It's honestly amazing.
There's also a survival mode, which is kind of similar to games like Rust and Minecraft, where you can fight zombies, while you build new things out of the surrounding materials, which consists of wood, rocks, plants, food, exc. You can even change your avatar to whatever you'd like, creating a lot of fun and uniqueness for friends. I don't know if i mentioned this either, but the game has a built-in voicechat feature, making it super easy for friends to play with eachother. I have 3 friends that i've been commonly playing this game with for the past few days, and we've straight up had an absolute blast playing around with it, and trying out all the different developer-made and community-made games, such as (in order of favorites) Gravity Gun Deathmatch, Shooting Range, Bar Fight, The Price is Right, Death Run, Prop Hunt, Hockey Rink, Open Roads, and more.
This game is really full of so many things, and I highly suggest you spend your $15 on it, and if you want to play sometime HMU on discord, my tag is HypnoStellar#0001. You'll really enjoy this game if you check it out, and give it a chance. Thank you to the developers for making it, it's brightened up my life and I've had a ton of fun playing it. Thank you!!

[h1]Experienced on the Oculus Rift and Windows Mixed Reality[/h1]

You can view my review & gameplay here: https://youtu.be/t1SHbtCY51U

So this is more of a modding software / sandbox than a proper game creation engine. As long as you accept the limitations of this tool, it can be enjoyable to make something yourself, even if it is ultra simple. However, this game / app would benefit greatly from some in-game tutorials that teach you from start to finish how to use the different tools available while making one of the featured games. 

The featured game creations are nice and you can sort of reverse engineer them. At least see how some of the different systems work. I especially enjoyed the sandbox aspect using some of the tools available. My favorite toy was the terrain making tool. I sort of felt like iceman as I ran along to areas where I was making new terrain. Then on the other hand, I had a gravity gun where I was grabbing explosive barrels and throwing them against the terrain to destroy it. Creation on one hand and destruction on the other equaled total mayhem. The game featuring these tools is actually a multiplayer game and it seems like it would be a fun MP game to play ... if anybody else was online to play with.

I never saw anybody online during any of my time with this game. So if you want to do any of the multiplayer features, you better bring a friend along. You can even create a game together or you can use the desktop version.

This app / game is running on the Unity Engine. I was getting anywhere from 45 to 90 frames per second on my 1060 GTX. The game did stutter at times. However, given the totally destructible environments and some of the cool tools, like the gravity gun, it's kind of surprising that this ran relatively well. 

My biggest criticism of the game, besides the lack of tutorials, is the poor controls. It uses a wheel system for tool selection that is just not very smooth or polished to use. While some experiences do have full locomotion, there is only snap turning available. On the Oculus Rift, that is mapped to the A or X button, which is never a good idea. 

Despite the problems with this tool, I did have fun. There's a surprising amount of variety with the different systems available to play with. You can even use ground vehicles or flying ones. Unfortunately, you do need to learn the scripting language in order to do anything other than very basic modding.

Once you get a map/game mode made and decide what you want to create and have it created the game itself is already half played before you enjoy what you made. For Oculus users if you have played Oculus Medium this game features a map making tool similar to it.
